name: Myrcene

pubchem.title: Myrcene
pubchem.description: Beta-myrcene is a monoterpene that is octa-1,6-diene bearing methylene and methyl substituents at positions 3 and 7 respectively. It has a role as a volatile oil component, a flavouring agent, an anabolic agent, a fragrance, an anti-inflammatory agent and a plant metabolite.

consumer_summary.what_it_is: Beta-myrcene is a highly aromatic monoterpene that gives many beloved plants their earthy, fruity, or clove-like scent. As a common volatile oil and flavoring agent, it is a molecule you encounter daily when peeling citrus, smelling fresh flowers, or enjoying a hoppy beverage.
consumer_summary.found_in: It is abundant in the essential oils of hops (Humulus lupulus), lemons (Citrus limon), and ginger (Zingiber officinale). You can also find it in fragrant herbs like rosemary, sage, and tea tree.
consumer_summary.why_researchers_care: Researchers are drawn to myrcene for its prominent role in the aroma and potential effects of medicinal plants, particularly cannabis and hops. They are actively exploring its potential to interact with receptors like TRPV1 and its broader biological activities. The strongest evidence so far comes from human observational studies (Oxford level 2b), which are investigating how myrcene-rich extracts might support joint health and overall comfort.

structure_function.statement: Early work points toward myrcene playing a role in supporting healthy inflammatory responses.
structure_function.basis: This is based on 6 papers, including human observational research.

structure_function.statement: Myrcene is being studied for its potential to support cellular health against oxidative stress.
structure_function.basis: This rests on 11 papers, primarily animal and human observational studies.

structure_function.statement: Researchers are exploring whether this terpene may support physical comfort.
structure_function.basis: This is supported by 5 papers, including human observational data.

structure_function.statement: Early evidence suggests myrcene may support relaxation and healthy sleep cycles.
structure_function.basis: This observation is drawn from 2 papers, including human observational work.

structure_function.statement: Animal research points toward myrcene potentially supporting brain and nervous system health.
structure_function.basis: This is based on 3 animal studies.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Researchers are exploring whether myrcene can act on pathways to support physical comfort, which could explain some of the soothing properties of myrcene-rich plants.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: This is currently being tested in an active, non-recruiting Phase 1 clinical trial (NCT04451863) evaluating the analgesic and subjective effects of terpenes in humans.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Because it is a major component of hops, scientists are investigating if myrcene contributes to the plant's traditional calming and sleep-supporting reputation.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A randomized, placebo-controlled human trial measuring sleep latency and architecture using polysomnography after isolated myrcene administration would clarify this effect.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Early animal work points toward myrcene potentially protecting neural tissues after mild impacts, raising questions about its role in brain recovery.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: The next step would be a Phase 1 human safety and biomarker study measuring neuroinflammatory markers in healthy volunteers taking a standardized myrcene supplement.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Researchers are curious if myrcene's presence in defensive plant resins translates to an ability to support immune defenses against environmental microbes.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A randomized controlled trial testing a topical myrcene preparation against a placebo for minor skin flora balance would help establish its clinical utility.

consumer_summary.cautions: In industrial settings, highly concentrated myrcene used as a solvent is an occupational exposure hazard, though this is not a concern at normal dietary levels.
consumer_summary.evidence_at_a_glance: Best evidence so far is human observational work (Oxford level 2b); most of the rest is animal and lab research.
